fix(dataplane): restore fks after copy unpartition of a partitioned sibling (#2787)

copy unpartition added a real foreign key onto event_deliveries or
delivery_attempts. postgres rejects that when the referencing table is
already partitioned, which is the path after retention drops _default.
the copy script now only drops the inbound key and installs the stand-in;
after-detach upgrades to a real fk when both sides are heaps.

fix(dataplane): reject empty endpoint_id on event match (#2788)

an empty api subscription endpoint_id must fail closed so events_endpoints never inserts null and the worker does not retry forever.

fix(api): invalidate subscription and filter caches on api writes (#2790)

cached.NewCachedSubscriptionRepository and cached.NewCachedFilterRepository
were constructed only in internal/dataplane/worker.go. Every api and dashboard
handler built the raw repository, so the invalidation those decorators
implement never ran in production. A subscription or filter edited through the
api left "subs_by_endpoint:<project>:<endpoint>" and
"filters:<subscription>:<eventType>" in place, and the worker kept routing and
matching on the pre-edit configuration until the ttl expired.

handlers now resolve subscriptions through subscriptionRepo() and filter
mutations through filterWriteRepo(), which wrap the raw repository in the same
decorator the worker reads through whenever a cache is configured.

filter reads stay on the raw repository. FindFilterBySubscriptionAndEventType
is read-through cached, not-found included, and the api uses it as a uniqueness
gate, so a stale entry there would reject a filter the caller is allowed to
create. every subscription read the api performs is a pass-through on the
decorator, so read-your-writes is unaffected.

invalidation deletes the shared cache entry. a per-replica in-process cache in
front of it still serves its own copy on replicas that did not handle the
write, so this narrows the staleness window rather than closing it fleet-wide.

fix(controlplane): invalidate endpoint caches on api writes (#2792)

cached.NewCachedEndpointRepository was constructed only in
internal/dataplane/worker.go. Every api and dashboard handler built the raw
repository, so the invalidation the decorator implements never ran for an api
edit. The delivery path reads "endpoints:<project>:<endpoint>" for two minutes,
so a retargeted url, a rotated secret, a pause or a delete kept being ignored
until the entry expired. This is the endpoint-shaped twin of the subscription
and filter gap fixed in #2790.

The six mutation sites now resolve through endpointWriteRepo(): create, update,
delete, expire secret, pause and activate.

That repository invalidates without ever serving a cached read.
UpdateEndpointService, PauseEndpointService and ActivateEndpointService load the
endpoint through the repository they are given and then merge or toggle onto
that record, so a read-through wrapper would let an entry up to two minutes old
become the base of the next write and silently revert whatever changed in
between. Handler reads stay on the raw repository for the same reason.

DeleteEndpoint also drops the endpoint's subscription list. That cascade happens
in SQL inside the delete transaction, below the repository, so nothing else
evicts "subs_by_endpoint:<project>:<endpoint>" and the match path would keep
routing to a deleted endpoint for the life of the entry.

The two-minute ttl is now the shared DefaultEndpointTTL rather than a literal in
the worker, so both sides of the same key agree.

perf(dataplane): cache subscriptions by source id (#2791)

FindSubscriptionsBySourceID was the last uncached reference-data read on the
incoming event match path, so every incoming event paid a Postgres round trip
the outgoing path had already been spared. It reads through the same 30s
entry style the endpoint-keyed lookup uses.

A subscription list cache is only correct if every writer evicts it, so the
existing writers now drop the source-keyed entry alongside the endpoint-keyed
one, and UpdateSubscription reads the stored row first: retargeting a
subscription onto another source or endpoint has to evict the list it is
leaving as well as the one it joins, and the pre-update row is the only place
those ids exist. A lookup failure there logs and leaves the old entry to the
TTL rather than blocking the write.

That pre-update read also closes the gap left open when the api handlers moved
onto the cached repository in #2790: an update that moved a subscription between
endpoints invalidated only the endpoint it joined, leaving the one it left
matching a subscription that had moved away until the TTL expired. It costs one
read on the dynamic-event ingest path, which also calls UpdateSubscription to
sync event types.

Two writers cannot go through the decorator, because both cascade delete
subscriptions in SQL inside their own transaction, below the repository. Source
deletion evicts the source-keyed list directly. Endpoint deletion collects the
distinct source ids of the endpoint's subscriptions before the delete, since
those ids exist only on the rows that are about to disappear, and evicts their
lists afterwards; #2792 already handles the endpoint-keyed list. Without both,
caching this read would let the worker keep matching subscriptions whose source
or endpoint is gone for the life of the entry.

fix(dashboard): Improve verify-email UX: auth shell layout and clearer modal (#2789)

* Improve verify-email UX: auth shell layout and clearer modal

* render /verify-email in auth shell without blocking bootstrap

* fixed verify email route

fix(events): use plain inner order by for paged exists scans (#2794)

Split LoadEventsPagedExists into InnerDesc and InnerAsc so generic plans can use events_pkey instead of a CASE sort key.

fix(dashboard): show the partition operation the button will run (#2796)

the table select's operation label could name the operation that suited
the previously selected table. selectedTable and selectedOperation read
partitionForm.value, whose aggregate trails a child control write, and
applyOperations runs inside that window off the table's valueChanges, so
switching to an already-converted table narrowed the operation for the
heap you left. reading the controls directly closes the window.

also drops the (selectedOption) handler on the table select: convoy-select
emits before it writes the control, so that call narrowed for the table
being replaced. the valueChanges subscription already carries the new one.

fix(controlplane): repair indexes postgres left invalid, rebuild them on demand (#2797)

* fix(controlplane): repair indexes postgres left invalid, rebuild them on demand

An index build that dies partway leaves the index in the catalog marked
invalid. The planner ignores it from then on, so the table performs as if
the index had never been created, and nothing said so: the only reader of
pg_index.indisvalid was the partition preflight, so the first sign of it
was a conversion refusing to start.

Nothing repaired it either. Index migrations build CONCURRENTLY, which
cannot run in a transaction, so a failed build is not recorded and has no
transaction to roll back. The retry on the next boot runs CREATE INDEX
CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS, which the invalid index holding the name
causes to be skipped, and the migration is then recorded as applied. 26
migrations build this way.

Repair is split, because the two halves cost very differently. Dropping
is instant and unblocks partitioning, so a migration does it and records
pg_get_indexdef first. Rebuilding is hours on a large table and must not
run at boot, so it moves to convoy utils indexes --rebuild, which resumes
rather than starting over and gives way to traffic on a lock. The same
convoy.drop_invalid_index makes future concurrent index migrations
retry-safe.

Losing a unique index costs more than speed: an invalid one is still
maintained by writes once it reached the validation scan, so it was
enforcing its key until the drop. The drop warns, the report says so, and
the rebuild order puts those first.

* fix: reset lock_timeout before returning the rebuild connection to the pool

a concurrent index build cannot run in a transaction, so lock_timeout has to
be set as session state rather than SET LOCAL. releasing that connection put a
3s lock_timeout into the pool serving ordinary traffic, where a row-lock wait
meant to queue would abort instead.

reset on the way out under a context of its own, since the leak's own trigger
is a cancelled caller context, and hijack the connection out of the pool when
the reset cannot be confirmed rather than hand back a poisoned session.

also stop the leftover-clearing drop from advising --rebuild: that path only
runs during a rebuild, so it named the command the operator was already
running.

feat(controlplane): rebuild invalid indexes from the admin dashboard (#2799)

an index left invalid by an interrupted build was reportable and rebuildable
only from a shell. this puts both on the admin surface, and makes "one at a
time" mean one for the instance, whichever page or shell started it.

convoy.partition_runs now records rebuilds alongside conversions: a
rebuild_index operation, an index_name column, and a CHECK tying the two
together. the partitions service grows StartIndexRebuild on the same insert
path, so a rebuild takes the single-active slot a conversion would, and the
partitions page's gate counts rebuilds or it would offer a start the server
refuses.

the guard enforcing that slot is itself a concurrently-built unique index, so
the repair sweep can drop it. checkGuard reads indisvalid and refuses to start
anything while it is missing, fail closed on a read error too. rebuilding the
guard is the one exemption, or an instance whose guard was dropped could never
recover, and that insert is serialized with an advisory lock in the same
transaction as the check, since the index that would have refused a second
starter is the one being rebuilt.

GET /ui/admin/indexes and POST /ui/admin/indexes/rebuild are instance-admin
only, matching the partition routes. no license gate: an interrupted build
leaves the same invalid index on an unlicensed instance.

the new page reports what is invalid now, what a migration dropped and still
owes, and flags a dropped unique index as no longer enforcing its key.
ListInvalid excludes anything already owed, so a failed rebuild is one row of
work rather than two. each list carries a known flag and a failed flag set only
by the catch, so an empty list before the first response is neither an
all-clear nor an error, and the start gates require the flag rather than the
absence alone: a poll that failed cannot report the shared slot as free.

the run card is extracted and shared with the partitions page. the partitions
sidebar icon moves to a copy of the grid glyph carrying no fill, since a fill
attribute on a symbol beats the class on the referencing svg.

feat(dataplane): add postgres as a first-class queue provider (#2795)

* feat(queue): add postgres queue broker behind provider registry

postgres now implements queue.Queuer with durable batched enqueue,
claim and completion, plus postgres-backed cache, rate limiter,
circuit breaker store and advisory locks. provider selection moves
into a constructor registry so consumers depend only on interfaces
and no longer branch on the configured provider.

lock holders use a dedicated bounded connection pool, and the lock
parameter is now an explicit max runtime that cancels the critical
section while holding the lock until the callback returns. redis
lease renewals fail closed by cancelling the critical section when
extend fails so a truncated singleton run is not treated as success.

* fix(queue): run postgres cron in utc and keep tick tombstones

the postgres scheduler used the robfig/cron default location, so cron
specs followed the host timezone while the asynq scheduler runs them in
utc. a spec like "0 1 * * *" fired at the wrong hour on any non-utc host,
and could skip or repeat a day across a dst transition. the scheduler now
pins utc so a spec means the same instant under both providers.

the finished cron row is what makes a tick idempotent across replicas,
but the archived-jobs cleanup deleted every finished row. that cleanup
runs on a cron minute other scheduled tasks can share, so it could erase
a tombstone a replica with a lagging clock was still deduplicating
against and let the tick run twice. finished cron rows are now retained
for a bounded window and aged out after it.

the tick id contract moves into the queue package so the scheduler that
writes it and the driver that matches it share one definition.

* perf(queue): write each postgres batch as one multi-row insert

writeBatch opened a transaction and issued one INSERT per job, so a
64-job flush window cost a BEGIN, 64 round trips and a COMMIT. Each
window is now a single INSERT ... SELECT FROM UNNEST ... ON CONFLICT
with no explicit transaction, since one statement is already atomic.

Per-job results come from RETURNING id: an id that comes back was
written, an id that does not is either an already-fired cron tick or a
job whose claim is still active. Duplicate ids within a window collapse
to the last request, which is what the sequential loop did anyway,
because ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE cannot touch the same row twice.

Measured on the write path alone, servers and agents stopped, 200
goroutines through PostgresQueue.Write, five samples each: 3,269 jobs/s
before, 13,204 jobs/s after, no overlap. The harness ships as
TestWritePathThroughput and skips unless PG_WRITEPATH_DSN is set.

* fix(queue): renew postgres claim leases instead of a 30-minute stuck timeout

A crashed worker used to hold its job for 30 minutes, because claimed_at
was set once and only the stuck sweep could undo it. The lease is now
renewed: consumers heartbeat every claim they hold, including jobs
buffered between the poller and a worker, so the timeout bounds how long
a dead worker's job is unavailable rather than how long a handler may
take. That drops the lease to 90 seconds and worst-case recovery to
about two minutes, in line with asynq.

The interval is deliberately six times shorter than the lease so a slow
database cannot expire a live worker's claim and hand its job to a
second consumer. Renewal outlives the poller and the consumer context so
claims stay held while in-flight handlers drain on shutdown, and it
skips rows that are no longer processing, which is how a released or
already-reclaimed job cannot be resurrected.

Also stop two scheduled tasks passing context.Background() to their
first repository call, which ignored the runtime bound the lock had just
established.

* fix(queue): close correctness gaps in the postgres provider

heartbeat timeout is now derived from the renewal interval instead of a
fixed 10s. at the 30s lease floor the interval is 5s, so a fixed timeout
could exceed it and leave roughly three renewal attempts before
ReclaimStuck takes the job rather than the five the design assumes.

the postgres cache no longer lets a concurrent Get resurrect an
invalidated key. Get samples a striped generation counter before its
read and skips the local Add if the stripe moved, so a Delete landing
mid-read is not undone. corrupt local entries are now evicted and fall
through to the table instead of serving a miss until TTL.

PostgresQueue implements io.Closer. write and complete batchers exit on
quit, buffered writes drain, and Write/Complete return errQueueClosed
rather than blocking on a drained channel. broker dependencies close the
queue so the batcher goroutines do not outlive a test.

advisory lock slot acquisition is bounded at 5s and reports ErrLockBusy,
so the billing usage recompute cannot starve cron jobs on the shared
pool. redis wraps its contention errors the same way, and the recompute
path logs contention at debug instead of labelling it a lock failure.

batch tracker rows carry db tags so the sqlx scan matches snake_case
columns. the e2e worker selects its consumer backend from the queue
type instead of hardcoding redis. the retry error message no longer
claims redis is required, and a compile-time assertion pins both
providers to the jobRemover interface.

queue tuning and cache local reads move into config with validation,
including a check that write concurrency cannot starve the connection
pool. the api integration harness passes the full broker dependency set
instead of four fields, so the postgres shard exercises the circuit
breaker store, acker, batch tracker and usage locker rather than
skipping them on nil guards. CI runs the api suite against both
providers.

* fix(broker): reject an unparseable redis sentinel database

the broker refactor dropped the error strconv.Atoi returns, so a typo in
CONVOY_REDIS_DATABASE silently connected sentinel deployments to database 0.

restoring the previous check verbatim would break the documented default:
convoy.env.example ships CONVOY_REDIS_DATABASE empty, BuildDsn reads empty as
"omit the database", and Atoi("") errors. treat empty as 0 and error only on a
non-empty value that will not parse.

* fix(controlplane): give each rate limit mount its own bucket key

the handler charged every request to the constant "http-api" key while being
mounted twice with different limits, once for the instance ingest rate and once
for the api rate limit. the two mounts shared one bucket, so each request was
charged twice and neither limit meant what it documents.

on the postgres limiter this is worse than mis-accounting: alternating limits on
one key thrash the in-process lease, which collapses throughput and stops
enforcement whenever the two values differ.

each mount now carries an explicit bucket. Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Reset
emit integer delta-seconds instead of a float and a unix timestamp, which
integer parsers rejected. limiter backend failures log apart from genuine limit
hits, since the two are indistinguishable in the response.

* fix(controlplane): split rate limit failure policy by surface

the limiter failed closed everywhere, so an unreachable limiter backend returned
429 on event intake and dropped ingest for as long as the outage lasted. that is
the wrong trade on a path whose entire job is to accept events.

intake now fails open: a backend failure admits the request unmetered, logs it,
and counts it as RateLimitOutcomeBackendError so the blind window is visible.
control-plane api routes keep failing closed, where rejecting is safer than
admitting unmetered writes.

the two policies need different mount points, so event intake POSTs move off the
project router onto /api/v1 behind the ingest limiter. a genuine over-limit
rejection still returns 429 on both surfaces.

* fix(queue): allow EventQueue to RetryEventQueue handoff while processing

Failed deliveries defer a write to RetryEventQueue with the same job id
while the EventQueue row is still processing. The conflict guard rejected
that handoff and stranded deliveries in Retry with no queue row.

Allow only the directional EventQueue to RetryEventQueue update, keep the
cron tombstone guard parenthesized, and block the reverse overwrite.

* perf(queue): cut per-event database work on the postgres delivery path

Remove three redundant lookups from the first-attempt hot path and make the
postgres queue provider's dequeue behaviour tunable.

- skip the match-path FindEventByID on first attempt; retries reload
- insert-first CreateEvent, dropping the pre-insert existence check
- carry an enqueue snapshot so first-attempt dispatch can skip
  FindEventDeliveryByIDSlim
- wake idle consumers over LISTEN/NOTIFY, with poll idle as the backstop
- env-tunable claim batch size, poll idle, lease timeout, batch size and
  write concurrency

At 1000/s offered with outgoing fanout 1, delivery mean drops from 86.3s to
67.2s and statements per event from 33.4 to 31.74.

Snapshot trust is gated on delivery mode. Lease reclaim and release return a
job to pending without incrementing retry_count, so a worker that died
mid-dispatch is redelivered with a retry count of 0. At-most-once therefore
reloads live status, letting the Processing guard refuse the second send;
at-least-once tolerates that duplicate by contract. An absent or
unrecognised mode is unknown and reloads too.

A duplicate-key create now returns the event alongside the error so the
caller applies the one status policy deciding whether match may run again.
Re-writing the deterministic match job for a row that is already Success or
Processing deletes and requeues it, which can fan out deliveries twice.

* fix(queue): honor at-most-once on processing reclaim and log claim batches

processingBlocksSend refuses resend for at-most-once when a delivery is
already Processing after lease reclaim; at-least-once still resends.

Postgres consumer logs configured pool/claim limit and periodic runtime
claim batch sizes so lab runs can verify effective dequeue batching.

* refactor(dataplane): drop dead code and dedupe the postgres queue provider

remove code with no callers: QueueNames, QueuePriorityCycle,
BatchTracker.UpdateProgress, ErrCacheConsume, a stored-but-unread
claimBatchSize field, the queueMonitorHandlers helper, and the
newPostgresJobLockerFromDB wrapper. drop the claim-stats benchmark
instrumentation and the opt-in write-path harness.

dedupe: one batch collector for the write and complete batchers, the two
Retry statements as named constants, isCountedFailure shared between the
redis and postgres consumer backends so both agree on which errors count
against the retry budget, an exported task.HeaderRetryCount, and
ResendClaimStore as an alias of the types package declaration.

drop abstraction that earned nothing: resolvedTuning becomes a
withDefaults pass over PostgresTuning, NewCacheAcker takes a
ConsumingCache so the consume requirement is checked at compile time
instead of asserted at wait time, and Monitor returns its handler
directly.

add CONVOY_POSTGRES_QUEUE_CLAIM_BATCH_SIZE and
CONVOY_POSTGRES_QUEUE_POLL_IDLE_MS to convoy.env.example and regenerate
the config reference, which also clears pre-existing drift.

tests: move the priority-cycle assertions onto queue.PriorityCycle so
they no longer need a database, and cover the retry path that had none
(TestRetryWithoutIncrementLeavesRetryCount,
TestRetryOnlyTouchesProcessingRows).

behaviour-neutral: build, gofmt, vet and golangci-lint clean, and the
failing-test sets before and after are identical (queue/redis and
worker/task fail the same way on origin/main).

* feat(dashboard): native queue monitoring for both queue providers

the queue monitor was an asynqmon iframe, which only exists for redis, so a
postgres instance had no way to see what was queued. this adds a
provider-agnostic queue.Inspector implemented by both brokers and a native
angular page that renders the same on either one.

the inspector serves its own status vocabulary, so the page builds columns and
filters from what the running provider actually has, and each task carries the
actions the broker will accept for it, so the page never offers a button the
update would reject.

the iframe goes with it: no fullscreen toggle, no minted monitor session, and
the admin container no longer widens for this one tab.

* feat: bring postgres queue monitoring to asynqmon parity

the native queue monitor now serves the same operations on both brokers:
throughput history with a per-day chart, queue pause and resume, run-now
and delete alongside retry and archive, bulk actions over a selection,
exact task id search, page size, auto refresh and a scheduler view.

postgres gains three tables for the state redis keeps inside asynq:
queue_state for pause, queue_job_stats for daily processed and failed
counts written in the same statement that completes or fails a task, and
queue_scheduler_entries where the in-memory scheduler publishes what it
registered. the claim query anti-joins queue_state so a pause applies to
every replica at once, and the nightly cleanup drops stat buckets past
the chart window.

bulk actions run per task through one shared helper so a stale selection
reports which rows moved and why the rest did not, and aborts instead of
recording an id-level failure when the broker stops answering.

* fix(dashboard): keep queue monitoring state across refresh and polling

the admin page read its active tab from the url but never wrote it, so a
reload landed on whichever tab the url happened to carry. writing the tab
back also lets the queue page persist full screen as a shareable link,
which needs the shell to merge query params rather than replace them.

full screen is a mode on the queue page rather than a wider admin shell:
sizing the shell per tab moved the sidebar when tabs changed.

auto-refresh no longer tears down what the operator is reading. a
background tick skips the loading flags and the row collapse, leaves the
last good page on screen when it fails, and does nothing while the tab is
hidden. an updated timestamp replaces the spinner it no longer shows.

charts now ask whether there is anything to plot. the history endpoint
fills every day in its window, so an idle queue drew an empty plot under
a date axis. bar heights also scale against their own track, so a
full-height bar cannot push its label out of the card.

* refactor: hoist broker wiring into ApplyToAPIOptions

Centralize copying broker-owned deps into APIOptions so server, dataplane,
and the API suite share one mapping instead of repeating field lists.

* fix(dashboard): restore asynqmon iframe for redis queue monitoring

Route queue monitoring by broker: postgres keeps the native inspector UI;
redis keeps the existing asynqmon embed unchanged.

* fix: harden queue monitoring auth and intake middleware ordering

read signing keys from cache before rng, gate native queue api on strict
instance admin, honor queue name in get tasks, and run project/org checks
before the ingest rate limiter so unauthorized callers cannot burn quota.

* fix(infra): split postgres queue migration index blocks for lint

Separate CREATE TABLE from CREATE INDEX in 1786696932.sql so mixed
index/DDL validation passes: transactional blocks for tables, notransaction
blocks for indexes.

* fix: wire e2e broker deps and drain postgres completions on close

E2E setups now build production broker dependencies via broker.NewTest so
StartConvoyServer and the worker get app.Broker. Postgres queue Close
drains in-flight completions like writes, and the worker pool warning logs
the effective max_open_conn value.

* fix: patch test broker cfg to testcontainer redis and db

Wire broker.NewTest through PatchTestConfig so E2E and cmd/utils tests
build cache, limiter, and circuit-breaker stores against the same
testcontainer handles as FlushDB. Restore cmd/utils circuit-breaker CLI
tests with full broker deps after the registry refactor.

* fix: align broker factory test with postgres queue monitor contract

Postgres broker leaves QueueMonitor nil and exposes QueueInspector instead; only redis requires asynqmon.

* feat(controlplane): gate postgres queue behind fflag and license

refuse to boot when postgres is selected without postgres-queue or
the postgres_queue entitlement. redis is unchanged and there is no
redis fallback.

* fix(controlplane): ping cache after pending migration check

postgres cache writes kv_cache, so a missing table must surface as
pending migrations rather than a cache ping failure.

* fix(dataplane): key postgres queue heartbeat on claim generation

status-only renewal let a stale worker extend a later claim after reclaim.

fix(migrations): reconcile endpoints NOT NULL schema drift (#2801)

Forward migration for name, url, http_timeout, and rate_limit_duration
brings CHECK-only fresh installs in line with long-lived SET NOT NULL DBs
so sqlc regeneration stays stable.

fix(dataplane): sweep orphaned events_endpoints after partition retention (#2800)

* fix: reclaim orphaned events_endpoints rows in retention

convoy.events_endpoints was in no version's retention set and nothing in
the tree deleted from it, so every row retention dropped an event for
stayed behind. It has carried no foreign key since sql/1724932863.sql
rebuilt it with LIKE ... INCLUDING CONSTRAINTS, which copies CHECK and
NOT NULL but not references, and an inbound key cannot be restored once
convoy.events is partitioned because Postgres refuses one that omits the
partition columns. A partitioned instance reached 4 GB and 18.6 million
rows this way while retention was otherwise working.

Partitioning the table was the other candidate and is not open to us:
it holds event_id and endpoint_id only, so there is no partition key
without a schema change and a backfill over the rows already there, and
an already-orphaned row has no event left to derive a key from.

The nightly partition retention job now sweeps the table after it
maintains the partitions that created the orphans. It reads a bounded
batch of rows whose event is in neither convoy.events nor
convoy.events_search, then deletes by event so a fan-out goes whole, and
repeats until the table is clean or a five minute budget runs out. The
read limits rows rather than distinct events because DISTINCT plans as a
HashAggregate under the limit, which reads the whole table before
returning a row.

Nothing records that the sweep finished, so a run cut short by the
budget cannot be mistaken for a complete one and an existing backlog
clears over successive nights on the same path. The sweep stands down
while a detach has not drained, since convoy.events does not hold every
event under the live name until the copy back completes and absence is
not a verdict there.

Closes PDE-1010

* fix: widen events_endpoints sweep conversion guard (PDE-1010)

The orphan sweep must stand down whenever absence from convoy.events or
convoy.events_search is not a verdict. Check convoy.partition_runs for an
active conversion and consult attach.Leftovers for split-table names
(_partitioned, _new, _old) on both event tables instead of only
events_partitioned.

Extract Leftovers in attach so conversion naming stays in one place.

* fix: re-check event table settlement each orphan sweep batch

Retention and partition conversion use different locks, so a conversion can
start after the sweep's initial settlement check. Re-check before each batch
and stop without deleting when tables become unsettled mid-run.

feat(controlplane): endpoint Teams notifications and transition-gated alerts (#2802)

feat(controlplane): add licensed event list search with exact JSON filters (#2803)

* fix(event-deliveries): join events on project_id for partition pruning

Without project_id in the events join, Postgres opens every events partition on the instance and hits shared lock limits (SQLSTATE 53200), breaking Event Deliveries on partitioned deployments.

* chore: treat empty HCP Vault config as unset and reduce tracer noise

Datadog entitlement shutdown in hooks, and stop logging unavailable tracing
as an error at init.

* feat(events): add licensed event list search with exact JSON filters

Implement unified Events log search behind EventSearch: text queries match

* fix(lint): shorten event list search swagger copy under the 300-char cap

drop entitlement language from query/body descriptions and remove unused hasQuery writes that failed ineffassign.

* test(events): cover list search on heap and partitioned tables

search without endpoints now uses payload containment on convoy.events
instead of events_search copy.

fix(dataplane): rewrite rollup days that already hold rows (#2810)

RefreshDailyCounts deleted a day range and re-inserted it in one
data-modifying CTE. Sub-statements of a CTE share a snapshot, so the
insert could not see the delete and collided on
event_delivery_daily_counts_pkey. The aborted statement rolled the delete
back with it, so the first write of a day succeeded and every later
refresh failed with SQLSTATE 23505. The every-minute job returns that
error before advancing the backfill, so completed_at stayed null and the
dashboard kept falling back to a live scan.

Split the delete and the insert into two statements in one transaction.
The insert upserts for the concurrent writer, and the range delete stays
so keys that no longer aggregate are reaped instead of left at a stale
count. Bounds are sent as pgtype.Date, which also removes a latent
$1::date shift through the session TimeZone on a non-UTC database.

Every existing rollup test refreshed a day exactly once on a fresh
table, which is why this was green in CI and failed on every run of a
populated instance. The tests now refresh the same day more than once.

Two further bugs surfaced while building end-to-end coverage:

- The job tracker read task.ResultWriter().TaskID() unconditionally.
  Only the asynq runner attaches a ResultWriter; the postgres runner
  builds the task from a queue_jobs row and leaves it nil, so the first
  delivery on that provider panicked and took the worker goroutine down.
- SetupE2E took the package mutex at the top and released it in a
  t.Cleanup registered much later. Any require in between aborts the
  goroutine, so a single setup error held the lock and every later test
  in the package hung until the timeout panic. The unlock is now
  registered immediately after the lock; cleanups run LIFO, so it still
  releases after teardown.

New e2e suites drive the admin surfaces added this month through a real
server over HTTP: the daily rollup read via the portal API, delivery on
the postgres queue provider, licensed event search, the boot index
rebuild walk, and the Prometheus scrape. The fast four run per PR via a
test_e2e_admin target folded into test_e2e_fast. Index rebuilds run real
CONCURRENTLY builds behind the instance slot, so they run nightly.

feat(controlplane): adopt orphan invalid indexes and block duplicate-key rebuilds (#2812)

* feat(controlplane): adopt orphan invalid indexes and block duplicate-key rebuilds

An index left invalid by a killed CONCURRENTLY build was invisible to the
repair path unless it already had a dropped_indexes row, so nothing ever
rebuilt it. Boot now adopts those orphans: it drops the invalid index and
records the debt so the existing queue picks it up.

A rebuild that fails on 23505 fails the same way every time, because the
duplicate rows have to be removed by an operator first. Those failures are
now marked blocked_at/blocked_reason on the debt row, boot skips blocked
names instead of retrying them on every chain, and an explicit rebuild
clears the marker once it holds the single-active slot. When the blocked
write cannot be persisted the process-local skip set covers the gap, and it
is only released after ClearBlocked succeeds, so a durable marker and its
in-memory fallback are never both dropped.

The admin index list and CLI report blocked state with its reason.

* fix(controlplane): bound adopt's drop lock and split the blocked-columns migration

the migration that defines drop_invalid_index bounds its own lock_timeout,
but that bound does not travel with the function. boot calls Adopt before
the listener starts, so the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE the drop needs waited forever
behind a long-running query on the same table, hanging startup instead of
failing open. bound it with SET LOCAL in a transaction, which keeps the
timeout off the pooled connection, and treat a lock we could not take as
busy so the rest of the list is still adopted.

split the blocked_at/blocked_reason columns out of the function migration.
the structure linter reads line by line, so the DROP INDEX inside the
function body cannot share a block with column DDL. the split also fixes
the rollback: reverse order now restores the previous function body before
the columns it writes are dropped.

fix(controlplane): give the concurrent index build its own lock budget (#2814)

* fix(controlplane): give the concurrent index build its own lock budget

a concurrent build waits for the table lock and also waits for
already-open transactions to drain, and it takes that second wait as a
lock on each transaction's virtual id, so one lock_timeout cancelled
both identically. the two are not the same risk: waiting for the table
means queueing ahead of traffic, while waiting for a drain costs only
time, since the build holds ShareUpdateExclusive throughout and that
blocks other ddl and autovacuum but not reads or writes.

with both on a 3s budget, any transaction open at the wrong moment
killed the rebuild. the daily counts rollup runs every minute and holds
one transaction for tens of seconds, so a rebuild only succeeded if it
started in a gap between runs. an observed instance failed the same
index on every attempt, waiting on Lock/virtualxid behind that rollup.

tableLockTimeout (3s) still bounds every statement that locks the table.
buildLockTimeout (10min) bounds the build alone and is restored to the
short value afterwards whether or not the build worked. the table lock is
probed first in its own rolled-back transaction, so a table someone
really holds is given up in 3s instead of occupying the single instance
rebuild slot, and the two failures stay distinguishable for whoever
reads the message. failures now name the blocker: holders and modes for
a locked table, pids with transaction ages for a drain wait.

perf(dataplane): validate ingest events without walking the payload (#2845)

govalidator validates a slice field by running the whole validator machinery
once per element, and json.RawMessage is a byte slice, so checking two required
fields on an ingest event cost roughly 560ns per byte of webhook body: 580ms to
615ms for a 1MB payload. ValidateStruct was 41.7% of agent CPU in the pipeline
profile.

The five ingest event structs now check their required fields by hand, with the
same messages, so validation is 8.4ns and allocation free at every payload size.
The valid: tags stay on the fields as the declaration, and a reflection guard
test derives a case from each one, so a new or changed tag fails until the
hand-written path enforces it.

Multi-field rejections now come out in field declaration order. util.Validate
built that string by ranging over a map, so the order was previously random.

CreateFanoutEventService called util.Validate directly, bypassing the model's
Validate, and it now uses the model with an explicit nil guard where the old
reflection error was doing that job.

perf(dataplane): cache verified api key derivations instead of deriving per request (#2844)

* perf(dataplane): cache verified api key derivations instead of deriving per request

NativeRealm derived a 4096-round PBKDF2 key on every authenticated request, so
the cost was paid per event rather than per key. A 30s CPU profile of the data
plane agent under saturating load attributed 31.08s of 102.49s samples, 30.3%,
to that derivation while managed Postgres sat at 17% of provisioned IOPS.

Cache only the derivation, which is a pure function of (key, salt), keyed on
both so a rotated salt is never answered from the previous derivation. The
stored hash is still compared on every call, including cache hits, and expiry,
revocation and role are still read from the API key row per request, so the
cache cannot carry stale authorization. Mismatches are not admitted, keeping
brute force at full cost and preventing wrong keys from evicting live entries.

Comparison moves from bytes.Equal to subtle.ConstantTimeCompare on both paths.

Verification per key drops from ~696us to ~330ns on the cached path.

* chore(dataplane): document that the api key cache index is not the verifier

sha256 here is the in-memory lru map key for a cached pbkdf2 output.
verification is still pbkdf2 at 4096 rounds, compared on every call
including cache hits.

feat(controlplane): report data plane depth on the queue monitoring page (#2851)

queue monitoring reads convoy.queue_jobs, so a deployment whose event path
does not run on the queue has no backlog surface at all: the page reports a
processed count and nothing about what is currently held or outstanding.

this adds a vocabulary-neutral contract for a data plane to describe itself.
a plane publishes named stages, named writers, named totals and named durable
backlogs into convoy.data_plane_snapshots, one row per replica, and the control
plane serves them to the dashboard. nothing in the contract, the store, the
handler or the UI names a component of any particular plane, so a plane can
change its own vocabulary without a migration or a UI change.

absence is unknown, never zero. a backlog carries its own known flag, a replica
that stopped publishing is marked stale rather than current, and no provider
answers 501 instead of an empty report, because an empty report reads as a plane
holding no work, which is the misreading this surface exists to prevent.

both routes carry the queue group's two gates, RequireAsynqMonitoring plus a
strict instance-admin check in the handler, matching the sibling queue reads.

also fixes the postgres integration harness, which could not compile: it called
a package-level log.Fatal that pkg/logger no longer exports, and its TEST_DB_*
variables never reached the configuration because nothing processed them.

feat(dashboard): rebuild the data plane panel around a verdict (#2852)

the panel was a wall of counters. every number reading zero looked

like, so a replica that had never accepted an event presented as fine.

the panel now opens with a verdict, then three numbers, then diagnostics
behind a toggle. absence and zero render differently: an unpublished
field shows a dash with a tooltip naming which absence it is, while a
field published as zero shows the zero, because a measured idle interval
is an answer. outstanding carries its retry schedule, and failures split
between work discarded before any attempt and work that failed after one.
data plane and queue share one tab behind a segmented control.

snapshot gains the shared throughput gauge vocabulary, emitted together
or omitted together, since a count without its window is not a rate.
deletesnapshot completes the store contract so a plane stopping on
purpose retracts its own row instead of waiting out the crash window.

two fixes found while testing it. maxconnidletime was applied only when
setmaxidleconnections was above zero, but that knob configures the
database/sql free list, so unset the pool fell back to pgx's 30 minutes
and one finished load run held 96 of 100 connections. three admin pages
rendered a licence claim from a flag they had not read yet, so every
load flashed a negative they then retracted.

fix(dashboard): say what a data plane replica actually counts as intake (#2853)

The intake number on a replica row is work that replica took on, and a
replica takes work on by more than one route: a client can send it work,
and it can pick up work that was already durable somewhere it reads.
Calling that number "accepted" reads as the first route only, so a
replica doing all its work through the second one looks like a broken
ingest, which is the misreading this panel exists to prevent.

The replica scope note went further and said work reaching the instance
any other way is carried by the queue. That is a claim about a
deployment the panel cannot see, so it now says only what a replica's
numbers cover and leaves how work reaches a plane to the deployment.

Copy, comments and test expectations only. The queue caveat beside the
segmented control is unchanged: the categories it lists still go to the
queue.

feat(dashboard): explain data plane diagnostics and prefer live replicas (#2854)

the diagnostics columns now say what an operator should do with each
number, including that unbounded is a mode. live replicas sort ahead of
stale leftovers so a restart does not open on a ghost card.

fix(dashboard): keep data plane stages table inside the viewport (#2855)

restore overflow-x-auto on the 640px stages table so a narrow viewport
scrolls the table instead of the page, and open the 375px spec against
the replica that actually owns those rows.

fix(dashboard): raise dropdown stacking and clip room for table row menus (#2856)

* fix(dashboard): raise dropdown stacking and clip room for table row menus

Row action menus were clipped by overflow-x-auto wrappers and rendered under table tooltips because dropdown panels used z-10. Raise overlay and panel z-index globally and add scroll-clip padding on every table wrapper that hosts row menus.

* fix(dashboard): scope table clip padding to row action menus only

Bugbot: pb/-mb on every overflow-x-auto table added phantom scroll below
pagination. Keep clip room only on endpoints, subscriptions, and team rows
with ⋮ menus; revert on filter-only table pages.

* fix(dashboard): size endpoint table clip room to dropdown max height

Match pb/-mb to max-h-[440px] so eight-item row action menus are not
clipped on the last table rows.

fix(dashboard): keep table tooltips visible without blocking row menus (#2857)

Add click-through table tooltips that stack above dropdown overlays and widen failure-rate hover targets so status and rate hints stay readable while row actions remain clickable.

fix(dashboard): widen fillHost tooltip hover target to component host (#2858)

* fix(dashboard): widen fillHost tooltip hover target to component host

Apply block w-full on the convoy-tooltip host when fillHost is set so failure-rate cells keep the full hover area Bugbot flagged on #2857.

* fix(dashboard): right-align fillHost tooltip toggles

Move end alignment to the trigger button so failure-rate labels stay on the right while the cell-wide hover target remains full width.

feat(controlplane): retention drop history in admin (#2859)

* feat(controlplane): retention drop history in admin

Record nightly retention runs with per-partition drop details and expose
them via admin API and dashboard UI.

* fix(controlplane): split retention_runs migration index block

Separate CREATE INDEX into a notransaction block so SQL migration lint passes.

* fix(controlplane): satisfy gocritic on adopted partition commit

Use short declaration for tx.Commit error check.

* fix(controlplane): keep retention history from blocking nightly drops

Snapshot failures are logged and recorded but no longer fail Perform or
retry Asynq after Maintain succeeds. Count rows only on partitions partman
marks expired, not every active child.

fix(controlplane): bound retention row counts so they cannot block drops

A slow COUNT(*) on the nightly job context can exhaust the asynq deadline
before Maintain and DROP run. Cap and detach those scans, and isolate
partition_runs in the boot-rebuild tests so leftover rows cannot inflate List.

fix(controlplane): separate retention and archiving entitlements (#2862)
